chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Influence on Kenton, Les Brown, Woody Herman and Johnny Richards
summary: Machito accepts that others borrowed from the band, but stresses Afro-Cuban jazz was a group creation by Mario and jazz players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Macho, there was some American band leaders, American pop band leaders like Les Brown. He recorded something called "Montuno Clipper" which was Afro-Cuban jazz. Woody Herman recorded "Bijou" in 1947, which could be considered Afro-Cuban jazz too. All these things after your "Tangana" was being played. Do you feel that the Machito

No question about it, it's no secret. If you are - let's talk about baseball - Hubbard, Hubbard create the screw ball, so every left-hander had to accept that pitching, with all the problem that physically you could ruin your arm, because in those days there was most right-hand hitters. In the major leagues, a good right-hand hitter in the major leagues that in any era, so you had to have the screw ball, the ball that it had the same effect like a right-handed, a curve ball for a right-handed hitter.
Did any of these band leaders, Woody Herman or Les Brown, ever call you or tap you for ideas, anything like that?

No, but you see, the American mind is very curious. Is a lot of people that consider an American watching a construction, that is silly, or because they could be entertained for a machine or a noise. They want to know because a year from now you just going through for any new construction and a year from now it going to be a big building, that you would never see the excavation that they made in order to make the foundation, so this is - ahhh - Everybody had in his mind architectural ideas.
Well, Stan Kenton was the first one to openly admit that he got the ideas from you. Are you familiar with Johnny Richards?
Now, he came after you. Now there were
a lot of things that he was writing which had the Chico O'Farrill, you know, touch. Do you think that you influenced Johnny Richards also?

Everyone. To me it was one of the greatest things that ever happened in my life. Be among people that could create such a thing because it wasn't my idea alone, it wasn't nobody's idea alone, it just one thing that there was a bunch of guys, with talent, with creativity, with flexibility, to say, well, let's cooperate ......
You are referring to your orchestra when they created Afro-Cuban jazz.

It wasn't Machito alone, it wasn't Mario alone. Mario, he light the foundation and from there Gene Johnson, Bobby Woodlen, the other guy and the other guy that it was following because they was the meat, they was jazz players.
